newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU tries to reassure aspiring new members.
newsitem.headline: EU tries to reassure aspiring new members.

text.p: The European Union sought to reassure a queue of anxious aspirant countries on Friday that their ambitions to join the wealthy western bloc would not fall victim to an internal EU power struggle.

Meeting leaders from 12 applicant countries to explain the state of the bloc after its recent treaty-writing summit, the EU was at pains to stress all would be done to make sure the EU is ready to take in its new eastern members early next century.

The message was in contrast to the pessimistic tones by European Commission President Jacques Santer and Dutch Premier Wim Kok on Thursday, who told the European Parliament failure by the EU's June 16-17 summit to agree on institutional reforms augured badly for the EU expansion project.

"If these countries are ready to proceed I do not think, there will be a delay because of the EU, because that would be a slap in the face of these countries and their people," Kok told a news conference after the meeeting.
"We have reassurances that these technical matters will not hold up enlargement, and for us this is the most important," Polish foreign minister Dariusz Rosati told reporters.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said there was still time to iron out the institutional changes -- on voting and the make-up of the European Commission -- necessary to prevent paralysis once the EU has up to 25 members.
At the summit, EU leaders agreed that expansion could only take place once the reforms had been agreed.
"It's going to be difficult to arrange...We have plenty of time to resolve this and we will resolve this," Van Mierlo told the news conference.

Leaders from 10 eastern European candidates for EU entry -- Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania and Bulgaria along with Cyprus and Turkey were at the meeting.
The meeting takes place as the eastern European countries nervously await the European Commission's assessment on July 16 of how suitable each of them is for the rigours of EU membership.

Concerned that the EU might decide to open talks with only five applicants to make its institutional adaptation easier, those acknowledged to be lagging in preparations -- like Bulgaria, Slovakia and Latvia -- urged the EU to set an equal starting date for negotiations for all, even though all might not join at once.
Commission President Jacques Santer said the EU executive would have different recommendations for each country.

"Even if they are based on objective criteria, most opinions will be different from country to country in that each country is different, some big, some less big...some have gone further with their structural reforms," he told the news conference.
Talks with Cyprus, which has already been judged to fit the bill, are due to start early next year.
Turkey's EU application has been shunned on human rights grounds and its presence on Friday signalled a renewed will on the part of the EU to make the secular state feel part of the European picture.

Kok stressed that while it was an applicant, it could not be considered a candidate for EU membership at the present time. "The status quo has not in any way changed following today's meeting," Kok said.
